lessons.title: The peoples of Cameroon and their movements
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 2 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the main groups of peoples of Cameroon
Describe the Bantu expansion in outline
Describe how oral tradition helps us to know about the past
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify the groupings of Cameroonian peoples used in the syllabus, the Bantu-origin statement ('several thousand years ago') and the examples named; classification of peoples is simplified.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: Long before Europeans arrived, many peoples lived in the area that is now Cameroon, with their own languages, chiefs, farming, crafts and beliefs. We can group them as: **Bantu** peoples of the coast, south and forest (for example the Duala, Bakweri, Bassa, Beti-Fang groups); **Grassfields** peoples of the western highlands (for example the Bamileke, Bamum, Tikar and many chiefdoms of the North-West); and peoples of the **north** (for example the Kotoko, Mandara, Fali, and, from the 1800s, the Fulani).

blocks.caption: Some peoples by region
blocks.alt: Three columns with example peoples of the coast and forest, the Grassfields and the north.

blocks.title: Bantu expansion
blocks.md: Linguists and archaeologists think the **Bantu languages** began to spread from the region around the present Cameroon–Nigeria border several thousand years ago. Over many centuries Bantu-speaking farmers moved south and east into the forest and savanna, taking with them farming, iron working and their languages. This was a slow movement of many groups, not one single journey.

**Why people migrated:** to find new farmland when soils tired or the population grew; to escape drought, war or disease; to find water, game or pasture; to trade; and sometimes because of disputes over succession. As migrants settled among others, they borrowed customs and languages, and the pattern of peoples we see today was formed. Many traditions say a founding ancestor led the group to a new homeland.

blocks.title: Oral tradition
blocks.md: Before writing was common, history was preserved by **oral tradition**: chiefs' lists, stories of founders and migrations, songs and proverbs kept by elders, court historians and palace officials. They are valuable but can be shaped by the teller's group, so historians compare them with **archaeology**, **linguistics** and written records.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Cameroon's peoples did not all arrive at the same time or from the same place.
- 'Bantu' refers to a family of languages, not a single tribe or kingdom.
- Oral traditions are useful evidence but need checking; dates are often uncertain.

blocks.title: Example 1: group a people
blocks.statement: Under which broad group would you classify the Bakweri of the Mount Cameroon area, and the Kotoko near Lake Chad?
steps: The Bakweri live on the coastal slopes and speak a Bantu language.
The Kotoko live in the far north around the Logone and Chari.
So Bakweri: Bantu coastal peoples; Kotoko: peoples of the north.
blocks.answer: Bakweri: Bantu coastal; Kotoko: northern peoples.

blocks.title: Example 2: reasons to migrate
blocks.statement: A community's farmland is exhausted and war breaks out nearby. Why might the group decide to migrate?
steps: Moving to fertile, safer land would help the group survive.
blocks.answer: Poor farmland and insecurity push people to move.

lessons.title: Chiefdoms of the Grassfields and the Bamum kingdom
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 2 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the organisation of a Grassfields chiefdom
Describe the Bamum kingdom and King Njoya's achievements
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: founding date of the Bamum kingdom (traditionally about 1400), the dates of King Njoya's reign (about 1889–1923) and the date of his script (about 1900), the spelling of local terms (Fon, Kwifon), and the list of chiefdoms.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: In the western highlands the people lived in many **chiefdoms** and small kingdoms. Each was led by a chief called the **Fon** (in the North-West; the term varies by area), who was both a political and religious leader and was respected as the link between the people and their ancestors. He lived in a **palace** at the centre, which was also a place of ceremony and art.

blocks.caption: Layers of authority
blocks.alt: A stack of layers from the Fon at the top to the people at the bottom.

blocks.title: Government of a chiefdom
blocks.md: The Fon ruled with the help of **councillors**, **titled nobles** and **regulatory societies** (such as the *Kwifon* of Nso), which made and enforced rules, settled disputes and could advise or restrain the chief. Villages and quarters were led by sub-chiefs or heads of lineages. There were also **age-grade groups** and women's societies that organised work and community life.

Well-known chiefdoms include **Bafut**, **Nso**, **Kom**, **Bali-Nyonga** and, in the West, many Bamileke chiefdoms (such as Bandjoun) and the **Bamum kingdom**. Their economy depended on **farming** (maize, beans, cocoyam, plantain), **crafts** (carving, pottery, ironwork, weaving, bead work) and **trade**, including exchange with neighbours of salt, oil, cloth, tools and later goods from the coast.

blocks.title: The Bamum kingdom
blocks.md: The Bamum kingdom, with its capital at **Foumban**, is traditionally said to have been founded about 1400 by a founding king, and was ruled by a line of kings. **King Njoya**, who ruled from about 1889 until 1923, is famous for creating a **writing system** for the Bamum language, setting up **schools**, a **museum**, a **map** of the kingdom and a large **palace**, and for encouraging crafts and learning.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Chiefdoms differ from place to place; not every Grassfields society had the same institutions.
- The founding dates in oral tradition are approximate.
- Palaces and art were symbols of the community's identity; many objects are today kept in museums.

blocks.title: Example 1: balance of power
blocks.statement: Why could a regulatory society limit the power of a Fon?
steps: The society made rules for the whole community and enforced them.
The Fon was expected to follow customs.
So the society acted as a check on him.
blocks.answer: Because it made and enforced rules the Fon had to respect.

blocks.title: Example 2: achievement of Njoya
blocks.statement: Name two ways in which King Njoya promoted learning in his kingdom.
steps: He invented a writing system for the Bamum language.
He set up schools to teach it.
He also kept records and a museum.
blocks.answer: He created a script and set up schools (and a museum).

lessons.title: The northern states, Kanem-Bornu and the Fulani

objectives: Describe the old states of northern Cameroon
Describe the Fulani jihad of the early 1800s in outline
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: date of the jihad (1804), the role of Modibbo Adama and Fombina, the names of lamidats (Ngaoundéré, Rey-Bouba, Banyo), and the Kotoko/Mandara descriptions.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: In the north, around **Lake Chad** and the Mandara Mountains, there were old states with markets and strong rulers. The **Kotoko** lived in walled city-states along the Logone and Chari rivers. The **Mandara** (Wandala) kingdom lay in the mountains. Both had contacts with the large empire of **Kanem-Bornu** to the north-east of Lake Chad, which traded across the Sahara and accepted Islam early.

items.text: North: from old states to lamidats

blocks.caption: Steps in the history of the north
blocks.alt: Four boxes from old northern states to the jihad and the lamidats.

blocks.title: Trade and religion
blocks.md: Caravans linked the north to Kanem-Bornu, Hausaland and North Africa. Goods included salt, cotton cloth, leather, ivory, grain and livestock. Islam, the Arabic script and ideas about government spread along these routes. Other peoples of the north, such as the Mafa and Fali, kept their own religions and ways of life in the hills and plains.

In **1804**, in Hausaland (northern Nigeria), the scholar **Usman dan Fodio** began a religious movement, or **jihad**, to reform Islam and rule. It led to the creation of the **Sokoto Caliphate**. Fulani leaders who joined the movement spread south and east. One of them, **Modibbo Adama**, founded the **Adamawa emirate** (Fombina), with its capital at Yola, and led conquests into the Adamawa plateau.

blocks.title: Lamidates
blocks.md: In northern Cameroon the Fulani leaders established chiefdoms called **lamidats**, ruled by a **lamido**, with capitals such as **Ngaoundéré**, **Rey-Bouba** and **Banyo**. They organised government, collected taxes, and the Fulani herders (with cattle) settled among farming peoples. Some local peoples resisted; some were included in the new states; relations were complex.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Fulani did not create the first states of the north; older states (Kotoko, Mandara, Kanem-Bornu) came before.
- The jihad was a movement in the early nineteenth century, not a modern event.
- Do not describe the northern peoples as a single group: there were many languages and religions.

blocks.title: Example 1: old states
blocks.statement: Name two peoples of northern Cameroon who had city-states or kingdoms before the Fulani jihad.
steps: The Kotoko had walled towns on the Logone and Chari.
The Mandara had a kingdom in the Mandara Mountains.

blocks.title: Example 2: the term lamido
blocks.statement: What is a lamido, and name one lamidat?
steps: Fulani rulers of northern states were called lamibe (singular lamido).
blocks.answer: A Fulani ruler; for example the lamidat of Ngaoundéré.
